body:
Akhyana in Gujarati literature and performance

Akhyana, also written as Aakhyan, is a narrative literary and storytelling form. In Gujarat, it became an important means of communicating religious, mythological and ethical stories through Gujarati verses, music and oral presentation.

Medieval Gujarati literature developed several forms through which audiences could understand narratives originally associated with Sanskrit texts. Akhyana helped present epic and Puranic stories in an accessible regional language.

Bhalan

Bhalan was a medieval Gujarati poet associated with Patan. He is traditionally described as the father of Gujarati Akhyana because of his important contribution to the development of this literary form.

His compositions include Dhruvakhyana and Mrugi Akhyana. His contribution represents an important stage in the development of Gujarati narrative poetry.

Premanand Bhatt

Premanand Bhatt was an outstanding Gujarati narrative poet associated with Vadodara. He developed the Akhyana tradition through accessible language, engaging characters and the adaptation of epic and Puranic stories.

His important narrative works include Nalakhyan, Sudamacharitra and Kunvarbainu Mameru. These compositions occupy a prominent place in the tradition of Gujarati literary and oral storytelling.

Maanbhatt storytelling

Maanbhatt, also written as Manbhatt, is a traditional Gujarati storytelling practice in which the performer presents an Akhyana through poetry, music, rhythmic narration and expressive delivery.

The distinctive musical instrument is the Maan, a metal vessel, commonly made of copper. The storyteller plays it rhythmically with ringed fingers while presenting the narrative.

Stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata and other Puranic traditions form a major part of the traditional repertoire.

The relationship between Akhyana and Maanbhatt is similar to the relationship between a narrative composition and a particular method of performing it. Akhyana identifies a literary narrative form, whereas Maanbhatt refers to the associated oral performance practice using the Maan.

Dharmiklal Chunilal Pandya

Dharmiklal Chunilal Pandya of Vadodara is recognised for his contribution to the preservation and transmission of Maanbhatt storytelling.

He received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 1983 and the Padma Shri in 2026. His work includes the presentation of traditional Akhyana compositions as well as narratives concerning contemporary subjects such as water conservation and environmental awareness.

These contributions illustrate how an established oral tradition can communicate new social messages without abandoning its basic cultural identity.

Oral epics of Gujarat's tribal communities

Gujarat's tribal communities maintain distinctive traditions of songs, ritual narration, oral epics and stories. These traditions preserve local accounts of heroes, kinship, community beliefs and cultural identity.

Bharath of the Dungri Bhils

Bharath is a major oral epic tradition of the Dungri Bhils of northern Gujarat. It has important narrative connections with the Mahabharata but also contains distinctive Bhil cultural interpretations and traditions.

It is transmitted through a combination of narration, singing, music and ritual performance. Its variations demonstrate that oral epics are not necessarily exact reproductions of written Sanskrit texts.

Scholar Bhagwandas Patel documented several oral traditions of the Dungri Bhils. The English translation of Bharath: An Epic of the Dungri Bhils by Nila Shah was published in 2012 by the Bhasha Centre and the Central Institute of Indian Languages.

Bhagwandas Patel's contribution was the documentation of a community's existing oral literature. He should not be identified as the original composer of the traditional Bhil epic.

Bards and community transmission

Traditional bards and narrators, including members of Charan and Bhat communities, have historically contributed to the preservation of genealogies, heroic legends, devotional narratives and accounts of regional rulers.

Community performers commonly learn their repertoire through observation, participation and instruction from experienced performers. Such traditions can include memorised verses as well as improvisation.

Recording oral performances in writing or audio preserves valuable material, but the survival of the living art also depends on continuing practice and transmission to future performers.

Prelims focus

  • Bhalan: associated with Patan and traditionally known as the father of Gujarati Akhyana.
  • Premanand Bhatt: Gujarati narrative poet associated with Vadodara.
  • Maanbhatt: oral storytelling accompanied by a metal vessel called Maan.
  • Dharmiklal Chunilal Pandya: Maanbhatt exponent and Padma Shri recipient in 2026.
  • Bharath: oral epic of the Dungri Bhils of northern Gujarat.
  • Trap: Bhagwandas Patel documented the Bhil oral epic; he was not its original traditional composer.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 7 Social Science, English edition, 2021–22, Formation of Regional Culture, p. 41; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10 Social Science, Literary Heritage of India, p. 31; Ahmedabad University, Intangible Cultural Heritage and Sustainable Development Workshop publication, section on Manbhatt Akhyan; Government of India, Padma Awards 2026 investiture citation, Dharmiklal Chunilal Pandya, p. 42, published May 2026; Bhasha Research and Publication Centre, Bharath: An Epic of the Dungri Bhils, publication details and description; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Gujarat's Oral Storytelling Traditions and Community Performers

body:
Theatre and storytelling as educational media

Theatre, puppetry and oral storytelling have traditionally served functions beyond entertainment. They communicate historical memories, ethical ideas, community customs, religious beliefs and social concerns to audiences through accessible forms of expression.

These art forms are particularly useful where an audience may not have access to written material. Visual action, spoken language, music and memorable characters help communicate ideas without depending entirely on reading ability.

Educational applications

  • Language learning: Dialogue, narration and repetition help learners become familiar with vocabulary and spoken expression.
  • Historical and cultural education: Dramatisation makes historical events, traditional stories and community practices easier to understand.
  • Moral and social education: Characters and their actions can illustrate the consequences of honesty, dishonesty, cooperation and discrimination.
  • Health education: Puppet shows and short theatrical performances can communicate messages about hygiene, nutrition and disease prevention.
  • Environmental education: Storytelling and theatre can explain issues such as water conservation and environmental protection.
  • Public awareness: Local dramatic forms can be adapted to communicate information concerning education, social equality and community welfare.

Why puppetry is useful in education

Puppets can represent human characters, animals and abstract situations in a simplified visual form. Through movement and dialogue, they can demonstrate a situation that might otherwise be difficult to explain to children.

A puppet may ask questions, make mistakes or encounter problems within a story. The audience can observe the consequences and understand the message through the narrative rather than through an abstract lecture.

Puppetry can also make use of locally familiar languages and characters. A simple glove or rod puppet performance, for example, can communicate an educational message without requiring a large theatre or elaborate stage.

Folk theatre and contemporary social messages

Traditional performance forms are adaptable. Their repertoire can be expanded to include modern problems while retaining familiar storytelling methods.

Gujarati Bhavai is an example of a theatrical tradition that uses humour and satire to make social concerns accessible. Maanbhatt storytelling similarly demonstrates how musical narrative can be adapted to contemporary environmental and social subjects.

These adaptations do not mean that the traditional art has lost its original identity. Instead, they demonstrate that living cultural practices may change in response to their communities' needs.

Preservation of living cultural heritage

Theatre and oral storytelling are important examples of intangible cultural heritage because their cultural significance lies largely in knowledge, skills, practices, expressions and traditions passed between generations.

The physical objects used in a performance may be tangible. A wooden puppet, painted cloth scroll, musical instrument or costume is a material object. The knowledge of making and manipulating these objects, the associated stories and the performance traditions are intangible cultural expressions.

Preserving the physical puppet alone does not ensure the survival of puppetry as a performing art. The associated skills, stories, music and methods of presentation also require transmission.

Role of community performers and institutions

Traditional performers are central to cultural preservation because they carry the knowledge required to practise an art. Family and community instruction, apprenticeship, educational workshops, public performances and documentation help transmit this knowledge.

Important institutions associated with the promotion, study and preservation of Indian performing arts include:

InstitutionRelevant role
Sangeet Natak AkademiPromotion, recognition and preservation of music, dance and drama
National School of DramaTheatre education and professional training
Centre for Cultural Resources and TrainingIntegration of cultural traditions into education and teacher training
Indira Gandhi National Centre for the ArtsResearch, documentation and preservation of cultural traditions

Distinguishing the major performance categories

CategoryPrincipal mediumExample
Classical theatreClassical dramatic texts and live performanceKutiyattam
Folk theatreRegional acting, dialogue, music and danceBhavai
Modern theatreModern dramatic writing and performanceIPTA productions
PuppetryManipulated figures or projected shadowsKathputli
Musical oral narrationSong, recitation and dramatic storytellingPandavani, Maanbhatt
Scroll storytellingPainted narratives with oral explanationPhad

These categories may share stories, music, costumes or religious associations. Their principal medium and distinctive regional characteristics provide a more reliable basis for classification than their narrative subjects alone.

Essential regional associations for revision

The geographical associations identify important centres of the traditions. They should not be interpreted as claims that each art form is practised exclusively within the named state.

Prelims focus

  • Puppetry and theatre can communicate educational messages without requiring literacy.
  • Bhavai uses humour and satire; Maanbhatt uses rhythmic oral narration.
  • CCRT connects cultural resources with education and teacher training.
  • Living performance skills and oral traditions are forms of intangible cultural heritage.
  • Traditional performance forms can adapt to contemporary social and environmental issues.
  • Trap: A puppet is a tangible object, whereas the associated puppetry knowledge and performance tradition are intangible cultural heritage.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Theatre Crafts, pp. 112–122; CCRT, Performing Arts, The Art of Puppetry and Traditional Theatre Forms of India; Ministry of Culture, Indicative List of Folk, Traditional and Indigenous Art; UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003, Article 2; Government of India, Padma Awards 2026 citation for Dharmiklal Chunilal Pandya, p. 42; official institutional information from Sangeet Natak Akademi, National School of Drama, CCRT and IGNCA; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
